## The Moon

The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite, a rocky body roughly a quarter of our planet's diameter that has circled us for some 4.5 billion years. The prevailing theory of its origin is dramatic: a Mars-sized protoplanet collided with the young Earth, and the debris flung into orbit coalesced into the world we see tonight. Because the Moon is tidally locked, it rotates exactly once per orbit, which means the same weathered face — its dark basaltic maria and bright cratered highlands — has looked down on every human who has ever lived. The far side, mapped only after Soviet probes photographed it in 1959, turned out to be strikingly different: thicker crust, almost no maria, a landscape of relentless cratering.

Its influence on Earth is far from ornamental. The Moon's gravity raises the ocean tides, and over geological time it has acted as a stabilizer for Earth's axial tilt, damping the chaotic wobbles that might otherwise have swung our climate through violent extremes. Culturally, it has been just as load-bearing — the basis of calendars, harvest festivals, and myth across nearly every civilization, and the destination that in 1969 became the first world other than our own to hold a human footprint. Those footprints, undisturbed by wind or rain, will likely outlast most of what we have built down here.
